changes: The "Outline Bar" is now called the "Outline Toolbar" everywhere it's named — the toolbar button, the View menu, and its tooltips. Nothing about how it works changed; just the name.
Outline: the checkbox in the outline view now reads "Use this variation in the outline toolbar."

Security: your Google Drive and OneDrive sign-in tokens now live in your operating system's secure store — the macOS Keychain, Windows Credential Manager, or Linux Secret Service — instead of the app's local storage. If you'd already connected a drive, the token moves there automatically the next time you launch; you won't need to reconnect. This keeps your cloud credentials out of plain text on disk. From the security review (D9).

The Notebook now tells you when it runs out of room instead of silently failing to save. If pages and pasted images fill the local storage it uses, you get a clear "Notebook is full" message, so nothing is quietly lost on the next launch. From the security review (D10).

A background error that used to only reach the developer console now shows a brief "something went wrong — your work is safe" note, so a hidden failure can't leave the app wedged with no explanation. (D14)
A corrupt or foreign file whose contents don't fit ScriptCraft's format now tells you so — and keeps whatever it could read — instead of opening as a silent blank page. From the security review (D8).

A Final Draft (.fdx) file with a garbled page size or margin value falls back to sensible defaults, instead of a bad number leaving the page unrendered. Same guard now protects the zoom and panel sizes from a stray non-number.

Reliability: saving a file is now atomic. If a save is interrupted partway — the disk fills up, a permission changes, a sync tool locks the file, the power drops — your file is left as its previous, complete version instead of being blanked or half-written. It writes the new copy alongside the old one and swaps them in a single step only once the new copy is safely on disk. This matters most for a Save-As'd or cloud-synced folder copy. From the security review (D3).
A size ceiling on opening files means a wrong or corrupt gigantic file reports "too large" instead of trying to load and exhausting memory.

Security: the app now only permits network connections to the handful of services it actually uses — feedback, the update check, dictionary downloads, and Google/Microsoft cloud storage if you connect them — instead of allowing a connection to anywhere on the web. If a bug or bad dependency ever tried to smuggle your work out to some other server, this stops it. Also removed a leftover allowance for the old Airtable feedback embed, which is long gone. From the security review (D11).

Privacy & security: link previews on the Beat Board no longer load on their own. A link in a beat now shows a "Load preview" button, and the preview — text and image — is fetched only when you click it. Before, opening a script from someone else quietly contacted every link inside it, which told the sender your device had opened the file and, with a crafted link, could even poke at your own network. Now nothing is contacted until you ask, and the app flatly refuses to load previews from private or local addresses. From the security review (D4).

Security (Windows): closed a hole where a specially crafted link inside an opened script's note could run a program instead of just opening in your browser. External links now go through the system's own URL handler — the same one File ▸ Print already uses — with no command shell in between, and they're limited to normal web and mail links. macOS and Linux were never affected. Found in the security review (D2).

Security: the PDF import engine (pdf.js) is updated to its latest patched release, closing a known flaw where a specially crafted PDF could run code when imported. If you import PDFs, this is worth having.

Security: the library that cleans up pasted rich text is updated to close a known sanitizer-bypass, and a small ID generator is patched too. No change to how anything looks or works — these are the known-vulnerability fixes from the security review.

Backup & Restore's hint is one paragraph now — the safety line follows "safe keeping" in the same breath instead of dangling under the checklist, and the odd line break after "shared between" is gone. The text was being wrapped at a width meant for the narrow hints under checkboxes.
The ribbon toolbar's how-to line sits below the Reset buttons — the true bottom of the Customize window.
The Customize window's section titles are set apart from helper text the same way the Settings window does it — small caps, muted — so a heading no longer reads as just another line of grey text.
The "Match the system's light or dark appearance" checkbox in Themes no longer touches its own label — the row had no layout at all.

Your fifteen-item pass over Settings and Customize, all in one go. The long explanatory paragraphs are gone or replaced with your short instructions — Themes, Context Menu, Elements, Transitions, the date and time formats, spell check, tabbed windows, and the Page Templates blurb.
Element Suggestions is Element Rules, with your helper line under it and the Show toggle up on the heading row.
The Customize window's Toolbar tab is Ribbon Toolbar, matching the Settings sidebar — and your how-to line now closes that window. Quick Access has its helper line too.

Backup & Restore reworded and re-spaced as you asked: your intro line with an empty row above it, Deselect All, both hints flush with their headings, the shorter safety line, and an empty row before the Restore button. Design and Helper Text are out of the backup list — their values live in the code now; a file you exported from either window still restores.
The New Script Picker's Shown/Hidden configuration is gone — a new script always offers every format. The old Script Format Preferences dialog and its first-run gate went with it.
The annotations panel's empty state now just says "No annotations yet."

The Enforce/Override hint in the template editor answers the question you asked: Enforce means the template's formatting is the rules, locked while writing; Override means it is the defaults, changeable while writing.

The app can install its own updates now. When a new version is out, the banner offers "Install and Restart" — it downloads the build, checks the signature, replaces this copy and reopens. The Download link stays right beside it, and it is still the only thing you get if anything at all goes wrong.

It only offers to install when the release really has a build for your machine. The button is decided by what was actually published for your exact architecture, not by "you're on a desktop" — an Apple Silicon Mac and an Intel Mac are two different downloads, and offering the wrong one would hand you something that cannot run. Your machine's identity comes from the Rust side, because Safari reports "Intel" on Apple Silicon and would answer confidently and wrongly.

Found while wiring it: the update check has been pointing at a repository that does not exist since v7.62, so "Check for Updates" has always answered "the update server answered 404". The automatic check swallows errors by design, so nothing ever surfaced it. Three things still have to be set up before an update can reach anyone — the public releases repo, the signing key, and a token — and docs/UPDATING.md lists all three.

One manifest serves both the banner and the installer, so there is still one version number in one place. A new Publish Update workflow builds all three platforms, generates that file from what was actually built, and publishes the installers before the manifest that names them.
The suite says out loud that the signing key is not set up yet, on every run, and refuses to let a release be cut without it.

Fix: editing a template's page setup now moves the script. Settings ▸ Page Setup ▸ [a row] ▸ View gives you a full page of margin fields, and pressing Apply used to save them to the template and stop there — so if you edited the margins of the template your script is already using, nothing on the page moved, the ruler's grey bands stayed where they were, and it still said "Page setup saved". Now, when it is the template this script uses, the measurements go onto the script the same way choosing a template does. A template you are NOT writing in still leaves the draft alone, and the message says which of the two just happened.

The rulers themselves were fine. The grey margin bands were measured off the canvas against every page setting there is — left and right margins, top and bottom margins, and page size — and every one of them tracks, at every zoom. They had nothing to follow because the page was not moving.

Your Design values are in the code now. All 81 of them are the tokens' own built-in numbers and the CSS defaults, so the app looks the way you set it with nothing overriding anything. Sixty-one values changed; the other twenty were already what you'd chosen.

Your helper text is in the code too — all 141 edits are now the actual strings in the app. The 45 you blanked have had their hover text removed outright rather than set to an empty string, so they stay gone once the Helper Text window is out of the release.

Both have been taken out of the shipped preset. A fresh install now starts with zero design overrides and zero helper-text overrides — the code says it, so nothing needs to be applied on top. That also means the Design window opens clean, and Export lights up only once you've changed something.

Fix: the Helper Text list was recording two strings the way the source spells them (with a \u2026 escape) instead of the way they read on screen, so an edit to either could never take effect. Both now match.
Fix: the check that keeps a Design default in step with its CSS couldn't see negative numbers — three of your ribbon gaps are negative, and it reported them as having no CSS at all.

Fix: the ribbon's untitled sections were sizing themselves against the wrong numbers. The maths that stretches an untitled section's rows to match a titled one read your OVERRIDES rather than the defaults, so the moment those values moved into the code it was working from a stale set — the rows came out 36px instead of 32 and spilled past their own padding, and the two untitled padding knobs stopped reserving the space they promised. The bar now measures itself the same way it paints itself, and renders pixel-for-pixel as it did in 7.75.

Ten checks on the ribbon's Design knobs had quietly stopped running: they found the Design window by looking for its row in the tool dock, and your profile doesn't put it there. They open it directly now, and all ten pass.

Fix: a popped-out window now sits on top of the side panels. It was drawing behind them — the Pages window in your screenshot — because a window lives inside the panel it was popped out of, and that panel was walling it in. The wall is gone; the window still covers the ruler, which is what the wall was originally for.

Outline presets lay down their sections and nothing else. Applying 3-Act Structure used to deal out sixty blank beat cards you had to clear before writing your own. The page budgets stay, and beats you've already written are still moved into the new sections and re-fitted — that part was working and hasn't changed.

Fix: clicking Freeform no longer makes a new outline tab. Freeform and Sections are two ways of looking at the same tab now, with the same cards either way, and each tab still remembers which view you left it in.

The Design window and the Helper Text window each have an Export… button now — Design's is in its footer beside Copy CSS, Helper Text's is at the top beside Reset. Each writes its own file, named so you can tell what's in it: scriptcraft-2026-08-22_design.json and …_helpertext.json.
Both files are ordinary preset files with one item in them, so they also import straight back through Settings ▸ Backup & Restore. Nothing new to read them with.
The button greys out when there's nothing to export yet, and says so on hover, rather than writing you an empty file.

Fix: opening a tool in a side panel no longer counts as a change to your workspace. “Save Changes to this Workspace” and “Reset to Saved Layout” stay greyed out for it. The workspace still saves and restores which tools you had open — that hasn't changed — it just doesn't treat looking at one as an edit. Closing a whole panel still counts, since that resizes the page and is something you'd arrange a workspace around.

You can now hide a workspace. There's an eye on every row in Edit Workspaces…; hiding one takes it out of the View ▸ Workspaces menu and out of the Workspaces panel, and Edit Workspaces keeps listing it (dimmed) so you can always bring it back. This is how you clear one of the five built-in workspaces out of your way, since those can't be deleted.

Your latest preset is in. The Default workspace's ribbon lost the two empty sections at the end and the alignment split moved up to take their place — 62 buttons now instead of 64. Everything else about the five workspaces is unchanged.
Your Default workspace now also opens the Feedback panel on the right — you had it open when you exported, and it's saved into the workspace. Tell me if you'd rather it didn't and I'll clear it.

Fix: preset and backup files were carrying a hidden marker that says "this machine already has the defaults". Yours did. Importing such a file into a brand-new install would have told it the defaults were already in place, so it would never have received them. The marker is now kept out of every export and refused on the way back in.

Fix: every Reset button was still putting back the old factory layout, not the settings you sent. Last version made your preset the defaults by writing them in at first launch — but the Reset buttons never read that; each one called a value written into the code years ago. So "reset to default" meant a default the app hadn't used since you sent me the file. That's why Customize ▸ Toolbar ▸ Reset gave you a bare strip of buttons.

Reset now puts things back to the workspace you're standing in. Reset the ribbon while Minimalist is applied and you get Minimalist's ribbon; do it in Outlining and you get Outlining's. Reset and "Reset to Saved Layout" can no longer disagree about what your layout is. This covers the toolbar, its size, the side panels, Quick Access, the right-click menu, and Reset All.

Things a workspace doesn't carry — your Design values, annotation presets, helper text, and the element and transition lists — reset to what the app ships instead. Resetting the element list used to un-hide everything; now it puts back the four you keep hidden.
With no workspace applied at all, reset falls back to what ships, and never to the old factory layout.

The app now ships with your setup as its defaults. A fresh install opens with your ribbon, your menus, your panel layout, your annotation presets, your design values and your five workspaces — instead of the assorted starting values it used to fall back on. Nothing you have already set is touched: this only fills in what has never been chosen, so your own app is exactly as you left it.

Workspaces: Default, Editing, Outlining, Focus and Minimalist ship with the app and can't be deleted or renamed. You can still rearrange any of them and save your changes over them, and you can still make, rename and delete your own. Renaming a built-in is off because the name is how the app knows which one it is — rename it and the original would come back beside your copy at the next launch.

Fix: all five would have shown “Save Changes to this Workspace” lit permanently. Your workspaces were saved before last version taught them to store fourteen more things, so the app compared what's on screen against a snapshot that had never heard of half of it and concluded something had changed. They're completed on the way in now, and each one reads as saved the moment you apply it.

A handful of things in the preset file are yours rather than the app's, and they were left out: your name and email, your folder locations, your Scrapbook, your bookmarks, and the window position — that last one is on a monitor to the left of your main screen, which on any other machine would open the app off-screen and look like it never launched.

The outline bar's scale slider is a light grey again, mixed from whichever theme you're on — so it picks up Gruvbox's warmth and Nord's coolness without being a colour of its own. Last version made it blue, which was my misreading of “fit the theme”.

Fix: “Save Changes to this Workspace” wasn't slow to notice a change — it couldn't see some changes at all. Popping a tool out into its own window, the panel item scale, the spacing between bars and the context-menu order were missing from what a workspace stores, so nothing noticed them and no workspace ever saved them. Workspaces now carry every customization the Customize window can make, so they save more than they used to as well.
The Production menu is hidden for now. Three of its four items weren't built yet; the fourth, Lock Scene Numbers, is still available as a ribbon button you can add in Customize.

Ribbon sections have a grip along their top edge in edit mode, so there's something to actually grab when moving one. The top strip used to be the title field, which has to take the click to let you type in it.

Fix: greyed-out menu items now say why they're greyed out — “Revision Mode (in development)”, “Lock Scene Numbers (scene numbers off)”. They were supposed to explain themselves on hover, and in the Mac menu bar they never could: that menu has nowhere to put hover text. The reason is in the name itself now, so it's there whichever menu you're looking at, with no hovering.
The Customize window's “Backup & Restore” button moved down onto the same row as “Lock All”. Both are about the whole window rather than the tab you're on, so they belong together.
The AI Writer tool is back.

Fix: Odia spell-check never worked. The dictionary was being downloaded from an address that has been returning “not found” the whole time, and a failed download looks exactly like a language you never turned on — so it just quietly did nothing. It now ships inside the app, like English already did, and works with no internet connection at all.

The outline bar's scale slider now takes its colour from whichever theme you're using — blue on Dark, cyan on Nord, purple on Dracula, gold on Gruvbox — instead of the plain grey it got yesterday. That grey was also far too bright: at the widths the slider actually takes, it was the loudest thing in the outline bar, brighter than the acts and beats it's meant to sit under. It's a tint of the theme's own accent now, a clear step quieter than the beats it scrolls.
The groove behind it gained a fine inside edge, so the slider still reads on the Solarized themes — their palette is deliberately low-contrast and has no room for the tonal step the other themes use.

Fix: the app icon was bigger than everything else in the Dock. macOS lays icons out on a fixed square and expects a margin inside it — ours was drawn edge to edge, so it rendered about a quarter larger than every icon beside it. It now sits on Apple's grid.

Fix: the outline bar's scale slider was inside out. The stretch between the two knobs — the part showing how much of the script you're looking at — was the darker piece, and the rest of the bar was lighter. It's the other way round now, and the middle is actually visible: it had been within a hair of the track's colour on every one of the twelve themes, so all you could really see were the two knobs.

“Save Changes to this Workspace” and “Reset to Saved Layout” are greyed out until you've actually moved something. Both do nothing when the layout already matches what was saved, in the Workspaces window and the View menu alike.
Customize… moved from the View menu to the Format menu.

Settings: the “Saving & Exporting” section is now “Save As & Export Windows”, because that is all it does — it sets the folder those windows are already sitting in when they open. Where your script actually gets written is the “Script Save Locations” section above it. Your chosen folder is unchanged.
A save you made yourself now just says “Saved” in the footer. “Auto-saved” still marks the ones the app made on its own, and hovering either still gives you the full date, time and which kind it was.

Fix: pop-up messages were close to unreadable on every dark theme. They were tinted from the script page's colour — which stays white when the rest of the app goes dark — so light text was landing on an almost-white bubble. Measured across all twelve themes, two thirds of these messages sat below the point where text stops being legible at all; none do now.

The ribbon's “⋮ More formatting options” button is gone, along with the collapsing behaviour behind it. A narrow window has scrolled the ribbon rather than hiding controls since v4.23, so the button was an escape hatch from something that no longer happens.

Workspaces: “Save current layout as…” is now a “Save as New Workspace” button sitting under the list, above “Save Changes to this Workspace”. Clicking it asks for the name in a window, and warns before replacing a workspace that already exists — the old text field quietly relabelled its button “Overwrite” instead.

Fix: the app would not start. Stamping the real version into the build last release wrote “7.62” where the desktop build requires three numbers — “7.62.0” — and it refused to launch rather than run with a version it could not read. The number is now filled out on the way in, and the check that is supposed to catch this looks at what was actually written instead of what it was given.

Fix: the Diagnostics report has been telling every reader the app is version 0.19.0 — the version this was forked from, three hundred releases ago. It quoted a number that no part of the app has ever set, so the one thing you'd paste into a bug report to say which build you're running was confidently wrong. It now reads the real version, the same one the About box shows.
The crate and lockfile versions were stale in the same way and now follow along, so there is one number in one place and everything else copies it.

ScriptCraft now tells you when a newer build is out. A quiet bar appears at the top of the editor naming the version and linking to the download; dismissing it means “not this one”, so the next release still speaks up. Help ▸ Check for Updates… asks on demand and always answers — including “you’re up to date”.

It notifies, it does not install. Installing a new build over a running one needs the app to be signed with an Apple Developer ID, which is still outstanding; until then the safe version is a link and a drag to Applications.

Fix: the version stamped into the built app had been frozen at 0.19.0 since that release. The About box read the real number so nothing ever looked wrong from inside, but every .dmg was labelled 0.19.0 — and it is the number an updater compares, so this had to be right before anything could be built on it. The release workflow now refuses a tag that disagrees with the app's version.

The footer shows when the script last saved, just right of its name — “Manually saved 11:04 PM” for a save you asked for, “Auto-saved 11:04 PM” for one the app made on its own. Hover it for the full date and time. A save made on another day leads with the date, in whichever date format you've picked in Settings.
Save As now counts. It writes the script through its own dialog and never told the rest of the app it had saved, so the most deliberate save there is would have left the footer blank.
Nothing is shown until the first save of the session, and a save time never carries over to a different script — a time belonging to the file you just closed would be worse than none.

The Ribbon Toolbar tab is back to what it was before v7.58: the palette of available items, and the real toolbar above as the editor. Drag items from the palette straight onto the bar, drag a section by its body to move it, hover an item or section for its ×, and use the bar's own “+ Add” for sections, dividers, spacers and the alignment split. The Shown/Hidden columns are gone.

Everything that came with that editor comes back with it — the highlight and dimming while the tab is open, the drag-to-resize grip on the dropdowns, the click-to-toggle dividers, section titles edited on the bar, and Cmd+Z to undo a ribbon change.

Kept from the versions in between: the greyed-out menu items still explain themselves on hover, the Editor tab's resets still sit under their own sections, and a column header's “+ Add” still sits beside its Show All.

The ribbon bar is highlighted again while the Ribbon Toolbar tab is open, so it's clear that the list you're editing is that bar — and that it changes as you go. Just the accent ring: the dimming that used to come with it was there to make the bar the only thing you could drop onto, and there's nothing to drop now.

The machinery behind the old in-place bar editor is gone — about 1,300 lines of drag handling, on-bar handles, the add menu and their styles, all unreachable since v7.58. Nothing you can see changes; the app just no longer carries a second toolbar editor it doesn't use.

The Ribbon Toolbar tab has the same Shown and Hidden columns as every other tab. It was the last one that didn't: it showed only a palette of what you could add, and you dragged from it onto the real toolbar, which turned into an editor while the window was open. Now the Shown column IS the toolbar, in order — drag between the columns, drag within Shown to reorder. Dividers, spacers, row breaks, section titles and the alignment split are rows in that list too, added from “+ Add” and dragged into place; a section title is typed in its own row, and clearing it deletes it. Dragging onto the toolbar itself is gone, and so is the dimming that came with it.

The reset buttons on the Editor tab now sit under the section each one resets, instead of in a single row halfway down the tab that looked like it belonged to Transitions. “Reset Mores & Continueds” is gone entirely — from Settings ▸ Defaults as well, so there is no copy of it left anywhere.

Fix: greyed-out menu items now explain themselves on hover. The Production menu's Revision Mode and Production Tags were given “This feature is in development” back in v7.06 and it has never once appeared — the styling that greys a disabled item also told the browser to ignore the pointer, so no hover ever reached it and the tooltip could not fire. Every greyed item says why now, and the ones greyed for a reason you can fix say what to do: Lock Scene Numbers points at View ▸ Scene Numbers, and a Bold or Align that the script format has locked says so.
The “+ Add” button in a Shown column header sits beside Show All at the right, instead of stranded in the middle of the header row.
Menu tooltips are listed in the Helper Text window, so they can be reworded like every other piece of helper text. None of them ever had been.

Fix: the Scrapbook's side panel showed twice — two copies of the same window, side by side, from the moment you opened it from the ribbon. The tool could hold two places at once: opening it floated it as a temporary window, and the Scrapbook then docked its own navigator, which seated it in a panel without the floating copy ever being told to let go. Each one drew the tool. A tool now vacates every other place it was when it takes a new one, whichever way it was opened.

Wherever a Customize tab lists Shown against Hidden, the button that adds to the list now sits in the Shown column's header, on the list it adds to, rather than in the bar at the bottom of the tab. Side Panels has a “+ Add” in each panel's header offering Divider and Spacer — and the left panel's adder adds to the LEFT panel now, which it did not before; Quick Access has the same in its Shown header. “+ New Theme” and “Add Transition”, renamed “+ New Transition”, moved to their Shown headers too.
The Continued Text and More Text dropdowns sit on one row. They are one decision — what the continuation markers say — and stacked down the page they read as two unrelated settings.
The Themes tab no longer ends with an empty action bar: “+ New Theme” was the only thing in it.

The Export… / Import… pair is gone from every tab in both the Customize window and Settings. In its place the Customize window has one “Backup & Restore” button below the tabs, which takes you to the Settings tab of that name — the one place that actually does it. The pair was never per-tab anyway: both buttons always moved the whole bundle no matter which tab you were on, so the Themes tab's Export… was exporting your toolbar layout too.

The Themes tab's own Export Themes… and Import Themes… are gone with them. Two things went with those: exporting a single theme as its own file, and importing themes out of another project — neither is something Backup & Restore does, so say the word if you want either back somewhere.
The Annotations tab's Reset now appears in Settings ▸ Defaults alongside every other reset. It had its own private copy and had never been listed there.

The bottom of every Customize tab is one action bar instead of three stacked blocks: what you can add to the list on the left, the tab's Reset and Export / Import on the right, with a rule above it and a hairline between the two. Quick Access, for example, went from three loose rows to one.

Fix: Export Themes… and Import Themes… were still stretched across the panel — they're sized to their labels now, along with the Continued Text and More Text dropdowns on the Editor tab, which were spanning the whole window to hold “(CONT'D)”.
The “Reset to Default” heading is gone. It sat above buttons that already say “Reset Items” and “Reset Transitions”.

Feedback submissions now record which app they came from. The feedback table is shared with Game Mastery and Fear the Reaper, so every row says whether it's a ScriptCraft report — otherwise three products' bugs land in one undifferentiated pile.

The buttons in Settings and Customize are sleeker. Most of them were stretching to fill whatever panel they sat in — “Hide All” was rendered 720px wide, Export… and Import… 613px each — so a two-word label sat marooned in the middle of a slab. They're sized to their own text now, on the app's compact button size, with one corner radius between them.

A button that asks to be the accent-coloured primary now gets it, wherever it sits. Dialog footers were repainting them plain, which is why the Customize window's Save carried its own colour rule to work around it.

Fix: clicking the lower part of a template card — anywhere in the wide empty space beside the View / Duplicate buttons — did nothing. A guard meant to stop a button press from also selecting the row was sitting on the whole width of that row instead of on the buttons. The whole card selects now, and pressing a button on it still doesn't.

Changing the format of a script that already has writing in it now asks first, naming the template and saying what happens: every element takes the new template's rules, and its page setup — page size, margins, headers and footers — replaces the current one. Both the Format ▸ Script Format / Template window and Settings ▸ Page Setup ask. Re-choosing the template you're already using, or picking one for an empty document, still goes straight through.

Settings ▸ Page Setup can now select a template and apply it to the open script, the way the Format ▸ Script Format / Template window does — click a row, then “Apply to Script”. It opens with the template your script is already using selected. Unlike the Format window it leaves Settings open afterwards and confirms with a message, rather than closing the whole window while you're still configuring things.

Applying a template is one shared piece of work now, so both windows do all of it: the template's page setup lands on the script, conflicts (an element the new template drops) are asked about first, and starter content is only ever seeded into an empty document.

Settings ▸ Page Setup now lists your templates exactly the way the Format ▸ Script Format / Template window does — each one showing its formatting mode, its description, and which template the open script is currently using — with a View button added to open that template's page setup. It is the same list, not a copy of it, so the two can no longer drift apart. The Shown / Hidden columns are unchanged, below it.

Every template row carries Duplicate now, including the built-ins (duplicating one opens the editor on the copy, since a built-in itself can't be edited). The old “New Template…” dropdown asked you to pick a base and then copied it — which is what Duplicate does — so it's been replaced by “+ Create Template” for starting from blank.

Fix: the per-template Page Setup window (Settings ▸ Page Setup ▸ View) had no Cancel — only Reset Default and Apply, so the only way out was to save or to dismiss the window itself. It has one now, and it discards your edits rather than quietly keeping them.

Internal: the engine that decides what the Font and Size pickers should be showing — reading the cursor, walking a selection, deciding when a selection is 'mixed', and finding fonts the document uses that aren't in the built-in list — moved out of the toolbar into one shared hook. Twenty-one browser checks cover it, including that a selection spanning two fonts still shows blank rather than silently picking one.

Fix: opening the Scrapbook's text-colour picker and then closing the Scrapbook left the script's text-colour picker sitting open. The two controls had shared a single open flag, for no better reason than that one function drew both of them.
Internal: the text-colour button and the Insert Table grid picker are their own components now, each holding its own state instead of borrowing the toolbar's.

Internal: the zoom control — the stepper, the editable percentage, and Reset / Fit Page / Max Width behind the caret — is its own component now, taking its state with it out of the toolbar. Nineteen browser checks cover it, including that Fit Page still fits ONE page rather than the whole script.

Internal: the Characters list — which names show, and in what order — moved into a tested function of its own. Fifteen tests now hold what was only a comment, including the reason Remove used to look like it did nothing.

Internal: the four import doors — this app's own files, Fountain/Final Draft/text, Word and PDF — moved out of the menu bar into one place, with tests proving each still asks before it replaces your open script. No behaviour changed.

Internal: Save, Save As and the "you have unsaved changes" question moved out of the menu bar into one place of their own, with tests covering the case that matters — a saved script whose autosave hasn't caught up yet still asks before anything discards your edits. No behaviour changed.

Seven dialogs — Go to Page, Open Recent, New Script, the launcher, the welcome screen, Choose script format and email verification — no longer lose your work if you select text inside them and let go of the mouse outside. They all now close on Escape too, which three of them never did.
The welcome screen and the launcher still can't be dismissed when there's no way out of them — adopting the shared behaviour didn't invent an exit they never had.

Internal: 429 lines of stylesheet that could never match anything are gone — rules for panels and controls the app stopped rendering versions ago. One Design slider went with them: "Panel title font" had been styling nothing since the panel header it targeted was replaced.
The app icon is rebuilt from the full-resolution logo, so nothing is upscaled at any size — including the largest macOS slot.

The app icon is yours — the SC mark. It's on the dock, the taskbar, the Windows tiles, the browser tab and the splash screen, generated from one source file so they can't drift apart. The last of the OpenDraft artwork is gone.
Internal: the cast reader — the code that works out who is in your script — moved out of the main editor file into its own hook. No behaviour changed.

Internal: the last of the editorStore split. Everything that describes the app's furniture — the ribbon's zones, the menu bar's order, the side panels' sizing and dividers, the chrome gaps and the right-click menu's arrangement — now lives in one file with the migrations that keep old layouts working. No behaviour changed; the store is 300 lines lighter.

The README describes this fork rather than upstream's: no more claims of real-time collaboration (removed in v6.40), no mobile apps this repo doesn't build, no download links to builds that were never published, and the setup instructions now cd into the directory the clone actually makes.
Odia dictionaries download from this project's own repository instead of upstream's.

Status messages — "Settings saved" and every warning or notice — now appear on the page where the Saved indicator does, instead of the bottom-right corner. They read the same measured spot the Saved flash uses, and stack under it when both arrive at once. If there's no page on screen (Statistics, the Beat Board, a fullscreen tool) they still use the corner.

Settings ▸ Save Options: the "Downloads" section is now "Saving & Exporting" and reads "Save and Export open in". Nothing in the app downloads — that folder is where Save As and every exporter open, which is what it says now. Your chosen folder is unchanged.
The transition "CUT TO BLACK:" is now "CUT TO BLACK." — a period, like FADE OUT.
The element suggestion table calls the row "Character Name", so it reads as the cue line rather than the person.
Removed from the context menu and from its Customize list: Insert Section, Insert Marker, Add To-Do List, Add Note, Revision Mode, Revision Color and Tag as…
Added to the context menu: Dual Dialogue and Insert Image — the two commands in the app that act on what you right-clicked and weren't offered there.
The "Your feedback has been sent" message sits half an inch lower.

Spelling & Grammar can live in a side panel now — it shows in the tool rail and in Customize ▸ Panels like any other tool, and still opens as a window if you'd rather. Nothing in the panel needed rebuilding: it was already built to fit a panel and was simply fenced out of the list.
Design… is in Help ▸ Developer. It's a developer tool, which means it's hidden from the tool rail and from Customize ▸ Panels — so until now nothing in the app could open it at all.

AI Writer is gone from the side panels. It wasn't Action Rewrite (that really was fully removed) — it was the joke panel from v1.69. Deleting a tool now also removes it from saved layouts, which is how this one kept coming back.

The Settings gear is #dddddd instead of pure white, matching the ink of the menu it sits in. The macOS menu item tints from the same value the in-app icon uses, so the two can't drift, and a theme change now repaints it.
The Settings gear is the solid one you sent (gear3.png), converted to white. Same size, same places — the menu bar item and the macOS app menu read the one file.

Fixed the giant gap above the first page: a Design value stored outside its slider's range was painted as-is, so a number no control could reach put an empty band above the script and nothing on screen could undo it. Every stored design value is now held to its own range wherever it is read — on the page, in the Design window's readout, and in Copy CSS.
If the gap is still there after this update, open Design ▸ Editor Surface and reset "Space above first page" — the slider can reach it now.
Asset Manager: the tags field shares a row with Cancel and Upload instead of taking a line of its own.

Settings ▸ Backup & Restore is now two sections that say what they do: Backup (tick what to include, save one file) and Restore (load one back). The old settings-only section is gone — it was left behind when Export moved into the preset window, with nothing under it but an Import button.
Restore reads both the new preset files and the settings files made before v7.28, deciding by what the file is rather than which button wrote it.

Housekeeping: 105 lines of styling for features that no longer exist are gone, and the tool that finds them stopped reporting 47 live ones as dead — it could not see class names the app builds as it runs, which is how the title page's styling ended up on a list of things to delete.

The Settings window reopens in the shape you left it — shrink it out of full screen and it comes back floating, at the size and place you put it. It reopened full screen every time before, whatever you did to it.
Tools already reopened in their last shape, full screen included, and now have checks holding that in place.

Every export door in the app now leads to the one preset window, with its own category already ticked and the rest one tick away. The Customize footer, Settings ▸ Backup & Restore, Export All Themes and the outline presets menu each ran their own separate export before.
Settings ▸ Import reads both the new preset files and the backup files made before this version, so nothing you exported earlier stops working.
Exporting a single theme still gives you a single theme file — a preset has no way to mean “just this one”.

Asset Manager: picking or dropping a file no longer files it straight into the list. The file is shown first, the tags box appears at that point, and an Upload button adds it with those tags. The tags field used to sit above the picker asking a question about nothing — and the answer applied to the next file rather than the one you had just added.
The Add and Library halves are separate, labelled sections, and the drop area has a border you can actually see.
Deleting an asset asks first, and says what is lost — a script using that file loses it, and there is no undo.
Assets can be renamed. The name on screen changes; the file on disk keeps its own name, so pictures already placed in a script keep working.

Dropping an image on the Asset Manager no longer takes the app down. It was not a glitch — a file dropped anywhere the app did not handle made the webview navigate to that file, so ScriptCraft was replaced by a plain page showing your image, and anything unsaved went with it. Dropped files are now caught everywhere; the Asset Manager's own drop zone works exactly as before.

The “Saved” indicator is on the page now — centred, about an inch below the ruler, and considerably larger. It is placed against the page itself rather than the window, so it stays centred when a side panel opens and its inch stays an inch when you zoom. Its size is a Design knob.
Verification: the checks a change can actually break now run on their own (`check-all --changed`), instead of all 91 every time.

The title page's draft date follows Settings ▸ Dates & Times. The date was stored correctly but written into the page as plain text, so a page built before you changed the format kept the old one forever — and Set Draft Number carried it forward onto every new draft. The line is rebuilt from the stored date now, whenever the setting changes and whenever a script is opened or imported. It is a display change, so it never marks a clean script unsaved.
Feedback: the attachment icon is gone and the label reads “Add a Screenshot:”.

A window opening while Settings is open closes Settings. Tool windows, the fullscreen takeover and every dialog. Confirmations and Settings' own pages — Page Setup ▸ View, Save As ▸ Save Options — leave it up, since those are Settings talking rather than something opening over it.

The gear in the macOS menu was never the icon you drew — it was macOS's own preferences gear. The app asked the dev server for your PNG and got a JavaScript file back, so the image failed to decode and the menu quietly fell back to the system icon. That is why scaling it did nothing. Your gear is in now, sized against the glyphs beside it.
File ▸ Open goes straight to the file explorer.
File ▸ Open Recent… sits below it and opens the list of your own scripts — the window that used to be Open. Its "Browse This Computer…" button is gone, since Open does that job now.
Open Recent shows your ten most recent scripts. Searching still reaches past the ten.
Each row shows its draft beside the name, so five scripts called the same thing are finally telling apart.
The Settings gear is the icon Derek drew — his actual file, not a redrawing of it. Both places it appears read the same image: the macOS menu item and the Settings entry inside the app.
In the app it is worn as a mask rather than placed as a picture, so it takes the colour of whatever theme is on. The file is white, which would have been invisible on the light themes.
Scripts are saved as .script now. Everything ScriptCraft writes — the copy in your chosen folder, auto saves, snapshots, Google Drive, OneDrive, and File ▸ Export — uses the new name.

Your existing .odraft files still open, and always will. So do the older .odraft.json copies. A file this app wrote is a file this app opens; the new name applies to new files, and nothing on your disk is rewritten or left behind.
What did NOT change is anything inside the file, or the identity macOS has recorded against every script you have already saved. Renaming those is what turns a rename into lost work.

Auto-saved files are named EpisodeX_autosave_08-15-26_23-15.odraft — no spaces anywhere, underscores between the parts, hyphens inside the date and the time. Spaces in a filename survive fine in Finder and then bite in a terminal, a URL, or a script.

The name no longer says what it is twice. It read "Auto Save — Episode X — Auto save — 08-15-26 23.15": the kind once from a prefix and once from the name itself. That prefix was also wrong for snapshots you take yourself — File ▸ Take Snapshot writes to the same place, so a snapshot you named came out labelled "Auto Save — …". It now carries the name you gave it.

Snapshots copied to Google Drive or OneDrive are real script files too. They were written as raw text under a .json name, the same fault the other copies had, so a snapshot fetched back from the cloud would not have opened. Every copy ScriptCraft writes anywhere now goes through one piece of code, and a test fails if a new one appears that doesn't.

The Google Drive and OneDrive copies had the same fault v7.18 fixed on this device: they were written as "<script>.odraft.json", holding only the raw text of your script without the wrapper the app reads. A script pulled back out of Drive would not have opened either.

Both now write the same real .odraft file everything else does. A Drive copy that already exists is renamed and corrected on its next save rather than left behind; a OneDrive copy is written under the new name beside the old one, and the old one still opens.

The copy ScriptCraft leaves in the folder you choose is a real script file again — and it opens. It was written as "Episode X.odraft.json": a name that looks like a ScriptCraft file but holds only the raw text of your script, without the wrapper the app reads — and File ▸ Open would not even offer it to you. The one thing that copy exists for, finding it later and opening it, was the one thing it could not do. It had been that way since the feature shipped.

Copies are now named "<script>.odraft" and written by the same code that writes the automatic backups, which had been doing it correctly all along. One feature, one folder, two pieces of code writing the file, and only one of them right.
The .odraft.json copies you already have still open — they may be the only record of what that folder held, so ScriptCraft reads them, and File ▸ Open now offers them.

ScriptCraft no longer asks your Mac for the run of your home folder. It had permission to read, write and delete anywhere under it — every file you own, not just screenplays — because a few features write to folders YOU pick and the file dialog doesn't grant access to a picked folder on its own. The permission is now the app's own support folder and nothing else; the writes to folders you pick go through ScriptCraft's own code instead.

Nothing about saving changes. Save As still proves a folder is writable while you're looking at it rather than failing later, the mirrored copy still lands in the folder you chose, screenshots still go to your screenshot folder, and dragging a file into the Asset Manager still reads it.

Two small repairs found on the way: a screenshot or a mirrored copy now recreates its folder if the folder has been deleted since you chose it, and the writability probe no longer depends on a permission that the narrowing removed.

The first line on page 1 no longer starts a line down the page. The blank-line-before rule was written for scene headings only, so a script opening the way most do — FADE IN: — began below an inserted blank, and so did one opening on ACT ONE. The rule is now stated once, for every element: whatever comes first sits at the top of the page. Everything below it is unchanged, so a heading after FADE IN: still gets its two blank lines.

The ribbon editor now renders the bar at exactly the size it will be once saved. Editing widened every section by 4px, pushed each one 8px further right than the last, and grew the two-row buttons from 43 to 48 pixels — so the bar you were arranging was not the bar you were going to get. Measured in both modes now, section by section and button by button.

A remove × that you cannot see no longer eats clicks. Each one hangs slightly outside its button, so at rest they were swallowing clicks meant for the section dividers beside them: you clicked the line, nothing happened, and nothing said why.

The Pages tool was drawing a page nobody would print. It kept its own copies of the text geometry under a comment saying they matched the real one; they hadn't for a while — scene headings took one blank line instead of two, and the right margin was 0.3 inches off. It reads the same numbers as the editor, the page count and the PDF now.

The Settings gear is the thin-line version, sized and weighted to sit among the macOS menu icons rather than beside them. The first cut was drawn bold and full-box; those glyphs are hairline and inset.

OpenDraft and FreeDraft are gone from everything a person reads — the setup and deploy scripts, the build scripts, the README and landing pages, all 25 user-manual pages, the GitHub issue templates, the security policy, the account emails, and the backend and collab server. 61 files, and a check that fails if a new one appears.

The download names were stale, which nobody had noticed: the app has been called ScriptCraft since v1.34, so the build has been producing ScriptCraft_0.19.0_aarch64.dmg while the release pipeline, the release script and every download link on the site still asked for OpenDraft_0.19.0_aarch64.dmg. Those now match. So does the version bump, which had been editing a package that no longer exists under that name.

What deliberately did NOT change, because renaming it would lose data or break a build: the 224 opendraft: storage keys behind every setting you have, the .odraft file format, the identifiers macOS, iOS and Android know the app by, the deployment environment variables, the service, volume and database names, and the Android signing keystore. The brand art keeps its filenames, the About window still credits OpenDraft as the upstream project, and the changelog still says what it said.
The Downloads tab is gone. Its two sections — where downloaded scripts go, and where screenshots go — are at the bottom of Save Options, Screenshots last.
Backup & Restore is its own tab at the end of the list, and the Presets section has joined it. Both are "carry my setup elsewhere", so they belong together; General is shorter for it.
Defaults sits directly above Backup & Restore. Keyboard sits directly above Ribbon Toolbar, which is what the Toolbar tab is called now.
Lock All is out of the Settings tabs and stays in the Customize window, where it was.

The Saved confirmation appears in the Quick Access bar beside the Save button instead of the bottom-right corner. A save is something you just did — the confirmation belongs where you did it. Failures still appear in the corner, because those you need to read.
In the Feedback window, the attach buttons line up with the paperclip above them when they wrap onto their own row, and "Your feedback has been sent" sits above centre rather than dead middle.

The Settings gear now reaches the ScriptCraft menu on macOS as the drawn gear itself, not a system substitute. If a platform refuses it, Help ▸ Developer ▸ Diagnostics says which icon was used — a fallback nobody can see is indistinguishable from nothing having changed.
Settings wears the gear you sent — an outline gear with eight teeth and a hollow centre. No icon set in the app had that shape, so it is drawn in the app's icon registry rather than approximated.

Its lines are white, and only its lines: the other icons in a menu are deliberately dimmer, so the gear stands out. On the light, sepia, paper and Solarized Light themes it takes the text colour instead — white on a light menu is an icon you cannot see.

Page Setup opens with a list of every template — View, and for your own templates Edit and Delete. The Shown and Hidden columns sit below it and are now only about visibility: a row there is a name and one toggle, and dragging between the columns sets what the New Script picker offers.

Settings has its own gear icon. It had been wearing the wrench that the Tools menu and every Customize… item also wear — three different things reading alike — and there was no gear anywhere in the app. The gear is used in the menu, on the toolbar button, and in the ScriptCraft menu on macOS, where it is the system's own preferences gear rather than a picture we ship.

The title page prints the draft date in the format chosen in Settings ▸ Region. The field stores a real date; it was printing the stored form (2026-08-14) instead of your format. An imported script keeps whatever date string its file carried — that text belongs to the file, not to us.
The Settings sidebar is one flat list of tabs — no System / Page / Customize captions or dividers.
"Keyboard Shortcuts" is now just "Keyboard" in the Settings sidebar.
Presets is a section at the bottom of the Defaults tab instead of a tab of its own — a preset is a saved set of defaults.

Page Setup manages templates in the Shown and Hidden columns the Context Menu, Toolbar, Side Panels and Quick Access tabs use. Drag a template between them, or use the × / + on its row; Show All and Hide All sit in the column headers.
Settings… in the ScriptCraft menu carries the system preferences icon.

Checked the five non-feature templates against their real formats. Radio Play was the feature layout wearing different labels — the character cue sat at 3.5" with the speech in the narrow screenplay column. Audio drama puts the cue at the left margin, the speech beneath it at nearly full width, double-spaced for markup. Fixed.

The 1-Hour TV Drama template is supposed to look like a feature script — hour-long teleplays are written in ordinary screenplay format — so its indents are unchanged. What it was missing is the structure that makes it a teleplay: every act now starts on a new page. Its scene-heading spacing had also drifted to one blank line and is back to the standard two.

Multicam Sitcom, Stage Play and A/V Script were already correct: capitalised action and double-spaced dialogue with an act per page; centred character cues and full-width dialogue; and the two-column video/audio layout.

Action Rewrite has been removed from the app. The tool, its editor extension, its stylesheet and the Rust-side API call and keychain storage are all gone — nothing about it ships any more. The About window's open-source list drops keyring-rs with it, since the OS keychain was only ever used to hold that tool's API key.
Extensions are on hold. The Extensions tab is out of Settings until the community-extension design is decided, rather than leaving a tab that offers nothing.

Page Setup ▸ View opens a full page of measurement fields for that template — page size, all four margins, header and footer margins, header and footer content — instead of a seven-line summary. It is the same page of fields as File ▸ Page Setup, pointed at the template.

Built-in templates can be edited too. Industry Standard, Multicam Sitcom, One-Hour Drama, Stage Play, Radio Play and A/V Script each keep their own page setup, saved separately so the built-in itself is untouched and Reset Default always brings it back.
Choosing a template now applies its page setup to the script. Without that the fields would have looked like they worked and changed nothing.

Exporting a title page to PDF now includes all of it — draft, contact, copyright, WGA registration and notes. The title page is laid out as a grid of lines, and the PDF exporter was adding a few extra points after every one of them, blanks included; across a full page that added up to two and a half inches of drift, which pushed the bottom block off the page. Anything that no longer fit was dropped without a word.

If a title page genuinely cannot fit — a very large title, a long contact block — the export now removes blank lines, starting with the widest gap, instead of dropping the text. Words never disappear from an export to make room for whitespace.

FADE IN: is left-aligned in the Pages tool, the way it already was in the script. The page thumbnails kept their own copy of the element measurements, with every transition pinned to the right margin; they now ask the same question the editor and the PDF export ask, so the opening transition sits at the left margin everywhere.

The character name suggestions list only names that are actually in your script. The list used to be a cache refreshed when the cursor crossed a name line, so a name you typed, left and then deleted stayed on offer — a stray "S" beside SCRIPTCRAFT. It is read from the script now, and the name you are in the middle of typing is never suggested back to you.

Pressing Enter at the start of a line puts the cursor on the new blank line above, not on the line you just pushed down. Adding something above a scene heading used to leave the cursor in the heading, so the next thing you typed — or the element you picked — landed on the heading and turned it into an action.
That same Enter is one undo step again. Inserting the line and setting the two element types were two separate edits, so one Undo took back only half of it.

Transition is offered on an empty page. FADE IN: is the opening transition and belongs at the top of a script, but the element list treated "nothing above" the same as "an unusual element above" and hid it.

The Languages tab is now Region, and it holds everything that depends on where you are: spelling language, inches vs centimetres, and the date and time formats. Measurements and Dates & Times moved out of General, which is now just Startup, Editing and Backup & Restore.
The Editor tab sits under Page in Settings instead of Customize. It's the same panel — only its place in the sidebar changed, and the standalone Customize window is untouched.

Settings opens full screen. It covers the side panels and the editing area and stops below the ribbon, so the menu bar and toolbar stay visible — previously it covered the entire app, including the window controls at the very top. The header's shrink button still gives you a floating window, and full screen re-measures itself if you resize the ribbon.
Removed the Draft Number section from Settings ▸ General. The draft label is still set from File ▸ Set Draft…
Add-ons are called Extensions.
Revision Mode and Production Tags stay in the Production menu but are grayed out; hovering either one says "This feature is in development."

Add-ons. Settings ▸ Add-ons is a new tab where extra features can be installed and removed. An add-on that isn't installed contributes nothing at all — no window, no menu entry, no toolbar option — and removing it puts the app back exactly as it was. Everything listed there ships inside ScriptCraft; nothing is downloaded.

Action Rewrite is now an add-on rather than part of the main app. It's gone from the tool rail, the Tools and Help menus and the toolbar customizer until you install it from Settings ▸ Add-ons. Your choice is remembered between restarts.
The Design window is a developer surface now: it opens from Help ▸ Developer and is no longer offered in the side panels, the toolbar customizer or the tool rail.

Removed about 730 lines of styling for controls that no longer exist anywhere in the app — 86 of the 309 orphaned styles found by the last update's check. The rest are held back deliberately: their names can be assembled while the app runs, so a text search can't prove they're unused, and deleting one of those breaks something invisibly.
The Design window had a slider — Outline title font — that moved nothing at all. The text it was meant to size hasn't been rendered by the app for some time. It's gone.

The About window's Compatibility table and the whole Grammar & Spelling Settings window styled themselves in code rather than through the app's stylesheet. Both now match everything else — and the error box in the Compatibility table, which was hardcoded light-on-white, is finally readable in the dark themes.
The tabs in Grammar & Spelling Settings are styled as tabs. They had been given button styling that every rule in the window then overrode.

Every control in the app now takes the app's own text size. Previously anything that didn't set a size fell back to the browser's default, which is slightly larger — this was measured before and after across the editor, all six Settings tabs and ten tool windows: only the window close button was still affected, and nothing changed size or moved as a result.

Removed a Light-theme override that was forcing a background onto every text field and dropdown in the app. It existed to rescue the controls that hardcoded a dark color, which is exactly why those looked correct in Light while showing up as black boxes in Sepia, Paper and Solarized Light. Those controls were fixed properly in the last update, so the override had nothing left to do — and while it stood it was overriding legitimate colors too.

The Grammar & Spelling windows (Settings ▸ General ▸ Grammar & Spelling, and the Dictionary Library inside it) look like the rest of the app now. Their buttons were raw browser buttons in every dark theme — those two windows built their own look in code instead of using the app's, so they never followed along. Fifteen buttons, the text fields and the headings now use the shared styles.

Buttons along the bottom of windows are one size. They ranged from 28 to 34 pixels tall depending on which window you opened — New Script, Guided Setup, the start screen, Spell Check and the confirmation boxes all match the standard now. Find & Replace and the two small popups use a proper compact size instead of being small by accident.

Dropdowns are one size. Ten different heights were in use, from 22 to 36 pixels; they share one size now, with a deliberate compact version in the toolbar where the row can't fit the standard one. The Characters sort dropdown was rendering at two different heights depending on where it appeared — same control, same list, two sizes.
Text boxes in dialogs are one height, and the Design window's Input height slider now moves all of them instead of only some.

Titles follow a scale: 16pt for window titles, 13pt for panel titles, 11.5pt for the section headings inside a window. Section headings are all muted gray now — they were split about half and half with full-white, so some headings shouted louder than the content under them.

Corner roundness is consistent — the side rail icons, zoom panel, welcome choices, Sticky Notes add button, Settings tabs and Tags create button were at six, seven and eight pixels against the app's four to five.

The zoom magnifier icons match the rest of the app's icon style, and the little stacked up/down arrows in the Workspaces window use the same control as everywhere else instead of their own smaller copy.
Removed an old, unreachable Settings screen that was still shipping with its own look, plus styling for controls that no longer exist.
Under the hood: a check that fails the build if a color is added to the app but forgotten in the Themes editor, and another that catches new styling with nothing using it.

Style audit fixes. Six theme colors were used by the stylesheets but defined by no theme, so about fifty hover, selected-row and background states quietly painted nothing: hovering a blue dialog button turned it transparent, the selected row in the Element Templates editor had an invisible highlight, and tool-window ⋯ menus, title-bar buttons, zoom menus and Design-panel rows gave no hover feedback at all. All six are defined now, in every theme.

Hovering a blue primary button keeps it blue. A specificity clash let the plain button's hover repaint the primary one; the plain rule no longer targets primaries, so one rule owns that hover in every theme.

Settings ▸ General no longer shows raw browser controls. Window on launch, Units, Date format and Time format were unstyled native dropdowns (19px, light gray) sitting beside the app's own; the Draft Number row had a native white text box and an unstyled 'Set as Default' button. All are house controls now, and the app declares its color scheme so no native widget renders in light style inside a dark theme.

One blue primary button style instead of two. Twenty-seven buttons used a paint-only class with no size of its own — it looked right inside a dialog's button row and like a tiny native button anywhere else (Settings ▸ Draft Number ▸ Apply). Small buttons are genuinely small now, too: the compact size set its font but never its height, so Page Setup's View and the Defaults tab's Reset stood full height with small text.

One red for danger, one green for success, one amber for warning — 117 hardcoded colors across the app collapsed onto three theme colors, so a theme (including your own custom themes) can change them. Annotation and index-card color palettes are untouched: those are your color choices, not app states.

Custom themes reach the whole app. Input fields, dialog surfaces, overlays, shadows, the edge line and the three new state colors are editable in Themes now — building a light custom theme on a dark base used to leave the input fields dark with no way to change them.

Deleting a formatting template asks first. The confirmation used the browser's own dialog, which in the desktop app answers 'yes' before you do — the template was deleted whatever you clicked. It now uses the app's confirm window.
The near-black boxes are gone from the Sepia, Paper and Solarized Light themes: eight search fields and dropdowns hardcoded a dark background instead of following the theme.

Housekeeping: the Thesaurus search icon matches the one used everywhere else, a duplicate button style that had been silently overriding itself was merged, dead Settings CSS removed, and the Script History diff labels use the app font.

Settings reorganized into categories: System (General, Save Options, Downloads, Languages, Keyboard Shortcuts), Page (Page Setup, Presets, Defaults), and Customize. The old System tab is gone, Languages has its own tab, and the new Downloads tab sets the default folder for downloaded/exported scripts — the Screenshots folder option moved there too.
The Defaults tab was rebuilt: every reset in the app is listed with a plain description of what it restores — now including the Design window, Helper Text, and Keyboard Shortcuts resets.
Settings ▸ Customize ▸ Toolbar stays inside Settings with the interactive toolbar editor embedded, instead of handing over to the Customize window.

Page Setup: the page-geometry block left the bottom of the tab — each template row has a View button that opens that template's page-size window. (Current-script geometry still lives in File ▸ Page Setup….)

Templates and Page Setup merged into one Settings tab, “Page Setup”. Templates are managed like themes now: Shown and Hidden lists decide exactly what the New Script picker offers, the six built-ins are marked Default (never editable or deletable), and New Template… creates your own — pick which existing template to base it on and the full editor opens on the copy. Custom templates appear in the New Script picker alongside the built-ins.
Settings gained a Customize-style footer: a blue Save that closes, and a Cancel that closes AND undoes every change made since the window opened.
Draft Number moved from Save Options to General, and Screenshots is now the last section in Save Options.

Settings sections: the titles moved inside the boxes (they sat on the border edge), the Design panel's Settings Window group gained a fifth knob so “Title to first item” and “Section top padding” are separate controls, and every Choose Folder… button right-aligns to the box edge, row to row.

The feedback box's list continuation is steadier: it now reads what's actually in the box (an internal lag could make Enter silently skip), and a bare “-” or “1.” with nothing after it counts as an empty item.

The settings section boxes now fill with a shade distinct from the window background, and the Design panel gained a Settings Window group: title-to-items distance, section bottom padding, section side padding, and space between sections — one set of knobs covering every tab.
The feedback formatting buttons are gone. Instead, typing “- ” or “1. ” starts a list that continues itself: Enter adds the next item (numbers count up), and Enter on an empty item ends the list.

The feedback Description box has formatting buttons — bold, italic, underline, bulleted and numbered lists. They wrap the selected text in lightweight markers that arrive formatted where the feedback is read.
Settings moved: it now lives in the Help menu directly below About ScriptCraft, with a divider on each side (it left the File menu). ⌘, still opens it.
The Settings window got a cleanup pass modeled on the reference screenshot from the feedback: every section is now a bordered group box with its name set into the border line.
Save Options: the auto-save timer and its locations are one “Auto Saves” section, and the tab's helper text is gone — only the Google Drive and OneDrive setup notes remain.
The ? and its explainer text are gone from the Feedback window, and the message field is labeled “Description:”.

Five more Feedback knobs in the Design panel: Type to its dropdown, Description to the text box, extra space above the attach box, the attach header's wrapped-row spacing, and extra space above Submit.
The Feedback window's attach buttons moved up beside “Attach a Screenshot”, with the ? at the end of the row, and the send button is simply “Submit”.

The Design panel gained a Feedback group with nine spacing knobs: the gap after “Name:”, name-to-Edit, label-to-buttons, between buttons, button-to-?, between rows, and the window's side, top, and bottom padding.

The Feedback window reads cleaner: “Name:” instead of “Sending as” (no email shown), “Type:” with its dropdown on one row, the message field is simply “Description” with no placeholder, the full-window capture button is “Full Screen”, and the area is titled “Attach a Screenshot”.
A ? beside “Attach a Screenshot” reveals the how-to on hover or click — the explanatory text no longer takes up room in the window.
The Feedback category choices are now Bug Report, Suggestion, Feature Request, and Other. (Praise is retired — put it in a Suggestion if you must.)
The Feedback form's attachment area is now labeled “Attach an Image” — naming exactly what the field accepts.

The Feedback form takes multiple attachments — the Screenshot, Area, and Browse… buttons stay put after something is attached, Browse… can pick several files at once, and each attachment gets its own removable chip.

Sending feedback confirms itself properly: the window blurs for a moment with 'Your feedback has been sent. Thank you!' front and center, then clears — replacing the small green note that was easy to miss.

Moving the Feedback window between the side panel, a floating window, and full screen no longer wipes what you've typed — the draft message, category, and attachment ride along with every move, and survive accidentally closing the window too. (Fixes the request sent through the feedback form itself.)

The Feedback form has a clear Attachment area — implementing the first request submitted through the form itself. Screenshot and Area capture now live inside a labeled box alongside a new Browse… button for attaching any image file from disk; whatever is attached shows as a chip with its name, a thumbnail, and a remove button.

Attached files upload in their real format (a JPEG stays a JPEG) and land in the feedback table's new attachments column. The table also gained a status column — Pending / In Progress / Complete — for triaging feedback in the Supabase dashboard.

Feedback sign-in is gone — replaced by a once-only tester profile. The first time someone opens Feedback it asks their name and email, remembers them, and every submission carries them. No codes, no verification emails, no external email services — friends-only testing on the honor system. (The verified sign-in from v6.84 stays in the project's history for a public release later.)
An Edit button on the form changes the saved name or email any time.

The reset buttons in Settings ▸ Defaults now warn first and can be undone with ⌘Z, exactly like the same buttons at the bottom of each Customize tab. They had been missed when the warnings were added in v6.77 — both surfaces now run one shared path, so they can never differ again.

Feedback is ScriptCraft's own now — no more Airtable. The Feedback window is a native form (category, message, screenshot) that sends to your private feedback database, and Help ▸ Feedback… opens the same window.

Testers sign in once with just their email: the app sends a 6-digit code, they type it, done — no passwords. First sign-in asks their name once, and every submission then automatically carries who sent it, plus the app version and platform.
Screenshots attach for real: capture the window or an area and it uploads with the feedback — the old copy-the-image-then-paste-it dance is gone with the iframe that forced it.
A submission that can't reach the server is never lost or silent: it lands in a visible local queue in the window, with a Retry button.

Ribbon customize mode: dropdown menus (Element, Font, Size, Editor View) can be resized by dragging their right edge — make them longer or shorter for formatting, and the live bar uses the same width.
Dividers in the ribbon toggle with a plain click now: click a dividing line to hide it, click the dashed ghost to bring it back. The × button on dividers is gone.

Settings ▸ Customize ▸ Toolbar now hands over to the real Customize window — the same live on-the-bar editing you get from the Customize button, instead of a copy inside Settings that could not edit the bar.
In customize mode the sections after the Align Split now hug the right edge of the toolbar, exactly as they will look outside of editing.

The ribbon's Show/Hide Annotations toggle wears a new pen-nib icon — distinct from the Annotations tool's marker, the highlight color's highlighter, and every other icon. The lit state still shows whether annotations are visible.
The “Drag to move this section” hover text in ribbon editing is gone — it collided with the other helper bubbles. The dashed section outline remains the drag handle.
When the Editor View dropdown sits in a two-row ribbon section, the “Editor View” caption is dropped — just the dropdown. Single-row sections keep the label.

Starting a comparison from the Script History tool's fullscreen view now works like every other path: the tool leaves fullscreen and seats itself into the side panel, so the comparison summary always appears there. (v6.80 covered the floating-window case; this covers fullscreen — the last way the panel could end up expanded but empty.)
+ Take Snapshot and Compare… now share the same blue button styling.

Starting a comparison now seats the Script History tool into the side panel itself. Before, if the tool was set to open as a floating window, the summary lived in that window — and on the Mac the window could fail to surface at all, leaving an expanded row with nothing under it. The summary now always has a real, fixed home in the panel while a compare is open.

The Compare… button sits beside + Take Snapshot at the top of the Script History window. The sentence explaining it (“Compare two snapshots side by side — pick two from the list”) only appears after you click Compare…, while you are picking.

Changing the draft number automatically files a snapshot of the script as it stood, named after the previous draft — change “1st Draft” to “2nd Draft” and a snapshot called “1st Draft” appears in Script History, its title page still reading 1st Draft. No snapshot is taken if the draft name did not actually change.
The snapshot list in Script History is compact now: one slim row per snapshot — name, age, and the View / Restore / Delete buttons all on the same line.

Picking snapshots to compare needs no checkboxes. Click Compare…, then click anywhere on a snapshot to pick it (click again to unpick); the second pick opens the comparison. While picking, the row buttons step aside so a click can’t restore or delete by accident.

The comparison summary’s box in the Script History window sizes itself in fixed pixels instead of a percentage — the likely reason it could come up empty on the Mac’s browser engine while looking fine elsewhere. The checks now also verify the summary’s real on-screen size, not just its presence.

Undo now covers ordinary edits made in windows, not just the big reset buttons. Retyping a helper text string (or blanking it, or its per-row reset), rebinding a keyboard shortcut (Clear and per-row Reset too — and a rebind that steals a key from another command restores both in one step), and changing a Design value all land on the same undo as everything else: ⌘Z takes the last one back, ⇧⌘Z brings it forward.
Dragging a Design slider counts as one change — a single ⌘Z returns to the value from before the drag, not one notch at a time.

Every button that makes a major change now shows a warning window first: Reset helper text, the Design window’s Reset all, every Reset in the Customize tabs (and Reset All), Reset Annotation Presets, Reset All Shortcuts, and the Helper Text window’s new Hide all / Show all. Each warning says what goes back to default — and names the undo key, because…

…Undo now reaches changes made in windows. ⌘Z (or the Undo button, or Edit ▸ Undo) takes back the most recent change wherever it happened — typing in the script, an outline edit, or a window action like a reset — and ⇧⌘Z brings it forward again. A window undo announces itself in a small message (“Undid: Reset helper text”), since the state it restores may not be on screen.
The Helper Text window: clicking Hidden now shows a bulk toggle beside it — Show all puts every hidden item back in the list, and when nothing is hidden it flips to Hide all.
